Its sound character comes from the physical properties of tape: the low end is full and round, the midrange warm and colourful, the top end carrying a soft magnetic sheen and a faintly retro feel. Against a pure digital synthesizer, it sounds more mechanically warm and more analogue. Its range is wide and can cover several octaves, and its way of resonating is distinctive: the tape loop running and the motor's vibration colour the frequencies naturally. Against traditional keyboard instruments it has more body and depth, with a typical analogue texture and period character, and is often described as nostalgic and artistic. The combination of mechanical running noise and electronic signal gives the instrument a distinctive sound personality.

The tape machine is an electronic keyboard instrument, originating in the German recording technology of the 1930s. It is a box-shaped machine fitted with playback heads, a motor and a tape-loop system. Besides being a recording tool, from the 1960s it was creatively adapted as an instrument by avant-garde composers, who used tape loops, varispeed playback and similar techniques in experimental music. Its timbre has both warmth and a mechanical quality: full low end, warm midrange, a top end with a soft magnetic sheen, a typical analogue texture and retro appeal, widely used in electronic music, industrial music and sound art.

錄音技術可追溯至1877年愛迪生留聲機；1886年貝爾實驗室有蠟紙帶機，1909: Recording technology goes back to Edison's phonograph of 1877; in 1886 Bell Laboratories had a waxed-paper-tape machine, in 1909 Goodell used celluloid sheets, and in 1932 Duston used light-sensitive paper tape. The idea of magnetic recording was put forward in 1878 and realised with steel wire by Poulsen in 1898; steel-tape machines appeared after the 1920s, and the BBC tried them in the 1930s. Around 1930 Germany developed tape recording with oxide-coated paper tape, in 1935 came an acetate base coated with iron oxide, and in 1962 Philips brought out the cassette machine. Tape made broadcasts and music recordings re-recordable and editable, and in the early twenty-first century it was largely replaced by digital.
